name: ATLAS
workload: Wall-clock time of dense matrix kernels from R-benchmark-25 run in R 3.2.4 (Microsoft R Open) linked to each BLAS, 10 runs: 2800x2800 cross-product and 2000x2000 linear regression; single-threaded ATLAS 3.10.2 (Debian package) against the Netlib reference BLAS, on Intel Xeon E3-1275 v5 and Xeon E5-1620 v4.
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded ATLAS 3.10.2 vs Netlib reference BLAS (chart bar labels and 'Performance gain' column in the README images): Xeon E3-1275 v5 2800x2800 cross-product 1.50 s vs 11.41 s (x7.6), 2000x2000 linear regression 0.747 s vs 5.466 s (x7.3); Xeon E5-1620 v4 cross-product 1.58 s vs 9.45 s (x6.0). Multi-threaded ATLAS dev branch 3.11.38 reaches 0.14 s (x79.3) on the E3-1275 v5 cross-product.
hardware: Intel Xeon E3-1275 v5 and Intel Xeon E5-1620 v4 (also ten other hosts in the same repo); Debian Jessie, kernel 4.4
stars_or_usage: 192 stars (GitHub mirror); SourceForge release 3.10.3 dated 2018-10-05; shipped as a Debian package
tradeoffs: Tunes itself empirically to the build machine (project description: 'applying empirical techniques in order to provide portable performance'); provides the BLAS API through C and Fortran77 interfaces but only some LAPACK routines.
caveats: The win is over the unoptimised reference BLAS only. In the same charts single-threaded ATLAS is slower than OpenBLAS 0.2.12 (0.49 s vs 1.50 s on the E3-1275 v5 cross-product), GotoBLAS2 (0.92 s) and Intel MKL (0.14 s), so it is not a fastest-in-class result. Numbers are read from bar-chart images embedded in the README (the page has no text tables); compiler and flags are not stated (the single-threaded build is the Debian package); 2016-era hardware and library versions; the suite is a small third-party repo (33 stars, Zenodo DOI) rather than a famous shootout. ATLAS's own timing pages (math-atlas.sourceforge.net/timing/) give DGEMM percent-of-peak (e.g. 89% on a 2.4 GHz Core2, ATLAS 3.9.5, gcc 4.2.3) without any baseline and its FAQ only makes qualitative 'competitive with machine-specific libraries' statements. The ATLAS papers (Whaley and Dongarra) were not reachable here (netlib and the author's site blocked). Project inactive since 2019; the last stable release is 3.10.3 (2018).
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: ATLAS listed in an awesome-c list (Numerical section) as 'Automatically Tuned Linear Algebra Software'; project home http://math-atlas.sourceforge.net/ has no baseline numbers, so evidence came from the WebSearch 'ATLAS vs reference BLAS dgemm GFLOPS benchmark OpenBLAS MKL' which surfaced andre-wojtowicz/blas-benchmarks

name: Caffe
workload: Time for a full forward plus backward pass of ImageNet-winner convnets averaged over 10 runs on one NVIDIA Titan X, using each framework's native (non-cuDNN) convolution kernel: AlexNet 128x3x224x224, Overfeat-fast 128x3x231x231, OxfordNet Model-A 64x3x224x224.
claimed_speedup: Caffe (native ConvolutionLayer) vs Torch-7 (native SpatialConvolutionMM), total ms per forward+backward pass: AlexNet 324 vs 342 (about 1.06x faster, derived from page data), Overfeat-fast 823 vs 878 (about 1.07x, derived from page data), OxfordNet Model-A 1068 vs 1105 (about 1.03x, derived from page data). Also well ahead of the OpenCL ports in the table (CL-nn 963 ms and Caffe-CLGreenTea 1442 ms on AlexNet).
hardware: 6-core Intel Core i7-5930K CPU @ 3.50GHz + NVIDIA Titan X, Ubuntu 14.04 x86_64
tradeoffs: Layer-based C++/CUDA framework with prototxt model definitions and a Python/MATLAB interface; cuDNN can be plugged in but the numbers above use the default native kernels.
caveats: Margin over Torch-7 native is only 3 to 7 percent. The same tables show Caffe (native) well behind TensorFlow (81 ms on AlexNet vs 324), cuDNN R4 through Torch bindings (81 ms), Nervana neon (87 ms), fbfft (104 ms), Chainer (177 ms) and cuda-convnet2 (177 ms), and on GoogleNet V1 Caffe is at 1935 ms against TensorFlow 445 ms, so Caffe is not faster than the modern baselines the lead names (TensorFlow, PyTorch). The README notes Caffe (native) and Torch (native) are only the default fallback kernels and that cuDNN can also be used through Caffe bindings. Benchmark is 2015-2016 era (cuDNN R2/R4, Titan X); compiler and flags for Caffe are not stated; Caffe has had no commit since 2020-02-13. The project's own paper (arXiv 1408.5093, 'over 40 million images a day on a K40', snippet only) was not reachable here (arxiv.org blocked) and gives no baseline numbers in the snippet.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: Caffe listed in awesome-cpp (Machine Learning) as 'A fast framework for neural networks'; README claims only 'speed' with no numbers; numbers from the independent soumith/convnet-benchmarks README (Titan X shootout) that includes Caffe rows

name: CatBoost
baseline: XGBoost 0.80 and LightGBM 2.2.1 (gradient boosted tree model prediction on CPU)
workload: Batch prediction of an 8000-tree model on the Epsilon test split (400K train / 100K test samples, 2000 dense features per the same repo's GPU benchmark README) with each library's own predictor, timed with %timeit (5 runs) at 32 threads and with a single run at 1 thread.
claimed_speedup: 32 threads: CatBoost 184 ms vs XGBoost 4.89 s and LightGBM 11.1 s (about 27x and 60x, derived from page data). 1 thread: CatBoost 1.98 s vs XGBoost 1 min 12 s and LightGBM 1 min 56 s (about 36x and 59x, derived from page data). Same repo, CPU training of 1000 iterations at depth 6 on Epsilon: CatBoost 266.77 s vs XGBoost 8935.36 s and LightGBM 1323.40 s; GPU tree construction on Epsilon: 17.9 ms/tree vs XGBoost 488 ms and LightGBM 40 ms (P100, 15 bins).
hardware: Not stated for the prediction notebook (run at 32 threads). The training-speed README in the same repo states Intel Xeon E312xx (Sandy Bridge) 32 cores for CPU runs and NVIDIA GTX1080TI + Intel Core i7-6800K for GPU runs.
tradeoffs: Symmetric (oblivious) trees give very fast evaluation; Python, R, Java and C++ APIs, native categorical features, GPU and Spark training. Training on CPU is not always the fastest (see caveats).
caveats: First-party benchmark with public notebook and scripts, but the prediction notebook states no CPU model, compiler or flags (pip wheels catboost 0.10.3 / xgboost 0.80 / lightgbm 2.2.1 from 2018), so tier C. The LightGBM predict call in the notebook sets no thread count. XGBoost and LightGBM have been optimised since 2018, so the ratio is probably smaller today. Independent training benchmark szilard/GBM-perf (2024) shows CatBoost slower than both on CPU (1M rows: CatBoost 7.0 s vs XGBoost 2.7 s and LightGBM 4.0 s; 10M rows: 70 s vs 40 s and 20 s) and slower than XGBoost on a V100 GPU (3.4 s vs 1.3 s on 1M rows), as summarised from that page; it does not test prediction. In the repo's own CPU training table CatBoost is also slower than LightGBM on letters (259.75 s vs 112.74 s) and airline (974.1 s vs 526.2 s). The repo README for the benchmarks directory itself contains no numbers; the model_evaluation_speed folder has no README.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: CatBoost listed in awesome-cpp (Machine Learning) as 'A fast, scalable, high performance Gradient Boosting on Decision Trees library'; README links catboost/benchmarks for the 'Best-in-class prediction speed' claim

name: FAISS
baseline: Babenko et al. CVPR'16 inverted multi-index search on CPU (Deep1B); Wieschollek et al. CVPR'16 GPU product-quantization search (Bigann)
workload: Approximate nearest-neighbour query time per vector on 1-billion-vector datasets with compressed codes: Deep1B (96-dim, 20-byte PQ codes, about 25 GB RAM, recall@1) and Bigann (128-dim SIFT, 8-byte codes, recall@10).
claimed_speedup: Deep1B at R@1 about 0.45: Faiss OPQ20_80,IMI2x14,PQ20 on 1 CPU thread 3.66 ms/vector (R@1 0.4561) vs Babenko et al. CVPR'16 on 1 CPU thread 20 ms/vector (R@1 0.45), about 5.5x (derived from page data). Bigann at R@10 about 0.35: Faiss CPU 20 threads 0.035 ms/vector (R@10 0.349) and Faiss on one Titan X 0.0340 ms/vector (R@10 0.376) vs Wieschollek et al. CVPR'16 on a Titan X 0.15 ms/vector (R@10 0.35), about 4.3x and 4.4x (derived from page data).
hardware: Faiss rows: 1 CPU thread, 20 CPU threads (CPU model not stated on this page), one Titan X; baseline rows are the figures published in the 2016 papers on their own hardware (Titan X GPU; 1 CPU thread).
tradeoffs: Library of many index types (flat, IVF, PQ, HNSW, FastScan 4-bit PQ, GPU variants); approximate search trades recall for speed, and compressed indexes need training and tuned parameters (nprobe, code size).
caveats: The baselines are numbers copied from two 2016 papers, not rerun on the same machine, and are research code rather than a library, so the ratios compare across different hardware. The CPU model for the Faiss rows is not stated on that page, and compiler and flags are not stated (last_commit is the v1.15.1 release date from CHANGELOG.md; the commit-list page was rate limited). The same wiki shows a library baseline beating Faiss: on SIFT1M nmslib HNSW takes 0.081 s at 1-R@1 0.8195 vs Faiss IVF16384,Flat 0.538 s at 0.8980 on CPU (the page says nmslib is faster but uses more memory; machines differ between tables). The wiki's FastScan-vs-ScaNN 1.1.1 comparison (1 thread, Xeon E5-2698) is only plotted in images and says 'faster and more accurate for all operating points before re-ranking' on SIFT1M, so no numbers were read; its '280k vs 140k QPS' HNSW comparison is against Faiss's own HNSW. The README's 'likely the fastest GPU kNN as of March 2017' claim comes from the GPU paper (arXiv 1702.08734), which could not be opened here.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: FAISS listed in awesome-cpp (Machine Learning) as 'A library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors'; README points to benchs/ and wiki; numbers from the Faiss wiki pages Indexing-1G-vectors and Indexing-1M-vectors
